content.comment:
+ Clarify the robustness and necessity of the proposed method.

As shown in Tab.7, our model outperforms the baseline in different levels of noise injection. We find that the performance gap is reduced when the noise level raises to 50%, and this may indicate that our model is less effective when the noise level is too high. This is understandable given such a hard case and we will add more discussions in the revision.

content.title: Clarify major misunderstandings and concerns
content.comment:
We thank all reviewers for their insightful comments and constructive feedback. Here, we want to clarify some main concerns and misunderstandings of our work.

+ Clarify the “complementary nature” of our designed method.

Correspondence modeling aims to predict whether a pair of video clip and text is corresponded or not in a binary classification format. Contrastive learning aims to learn a common embedding space for both video clip and text in an instance discrimination manner. As can be seen, correspondence modeling is a more weak supervision signal by learning a decision boundary without mapping different modalities into the same space under distance constraints. It has been validated through our experiments in Sec.3.4 that the correspondence modeling can complement contrastive learning which has a powerful representation learning ability for better training from noisy web data. We guess the underlying reason is that correspondence modeling is a more reliable supervision signal as a visual-text pair can be correlated/corresponded without being necessary to close with each other in embedding space. Or in other words, correspondence modeling helps learn a complementary space for finding correlations between video and text. We would like to clarify this in the revision.

+ Clarify the concept of “co-training”.

The co-training in our context means calibrating contrastive loss while learning correspondence, which is apparently different from the one in semi-supervised learning that utilizes partially labelled data for joint training. We will avoid using such confusing words and revise the related sentences. 
Besides, our Sec.3 targets on a preliminary study for examining the effectiveness of three different losses in our task. When we train the three losses together, the parameters are set for stable training given the different scales of each loss, which is a common way for machine learning when multiple losses are involved.

+ Clarify “ours” and “R@” in result tables, and $\hat{c_{ii}}$.

As introduced clearly in Sec.4, ours indicates Eq.6. Note that Sec.3 is mainly served for analysis and preliminary study of our task. We use metrics of R@ for retrieval tasks following previous works which are quite commonly used, while accuracy aims to measure the action recognition task. As for $\hat{c_{ii}}$, it is defined in Sec.3.1 and is obtained by the correspondence branch trained from the last epoch.

+ Clarify the comparison with baselines.

With the rapid development of this area, methods with various experimental settings come out quickly and authors update their papers (on arXiv) in a very timely manner. For example, for the “Frozen in Time” paper, we apologize that we refer to the numbers from their first version on arXiv without continuously checking their latest version, and we will keep it updated in the revision. Note that even compare to its latest version ([v2]), our model still outperforms it, as shown in Tab.6 (32.9 vs. 24.7 for R@1). Since previous works use different backbones for training and the performance gap between CNN-based and Transformer-based models is quite large, we conduct the experiments on different backbones respectively for fairness. Our experiments mainly show results on the CNN-based model given the limited computational resources available, such as the one on HMDB. Thus, we argue that the work [1] mentioned by Reviewer Jb8i should not be used to compare with our model in this case. And the same reason for comparing zero-shot retrieval from our model to the work of [2]. Besides, for CLIP, to fairly compare, we use the exact same setting as the baseline and demonstrate the effectiveness of our model in Tab.6. And the reviewers t1gW and Jb8i ask the comparison to an arXiv paper without undergoing a peer-reviewed process violates the review policy.
 
+ Clarify the comparison with a related work [Robust Audio-Visual Instance Discrimination].

We acknowledge that the “reweighting” scheme is not that new as it has been widely used in many machine learning algorithms as a general concept. But we argue that the way we re-weight the loss is new, especially in comparison to the above-mentioned work. In the above work, they use the dot-product of the audio and video features to get a similarity score and then reweight their loss according to (a cumulation of) this score. Whereas in our work, we use the corresponding modeling to calculate the calibration score for the reweighting, which was shown to be effective through extensive experiments. In summary, we are addressing a similar challenge (within cross-modal modelling) from different perspectives and using different technical approaches.
Besides, the paper mentioned above (and other cross-model learning methods) is mainly about *audio* and video, while our work focuses on *text* and video. They seem to be within the same category of cross-modal data, but with essentially different properties by nature (text vs. audio).

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a cross-modal video representation learning that serves as a pre-trained model for downstream tasks.  The authors propose a visual-language model that aligns visual features and textual semantics.  Specifically, this paper presents to train the model on large-scale web videos with noisy captions (WebVid-2M) using three losses -- cross entropy loss for correspondence modeling, contrastive loss for visual-textual contrastive learning, and mean square loss for predictive coding.  A weighted sum of contrastive loss and cross-entropy loss is proposed and termed as Cali-NCE, with the purpose to reduce false positive/negative visual-semantic pairs (i.e., videos vs captions).  Experiments are conducted on three downstream tasks including text-to-video retrieval, video action recognition, and video-to-video retrieval.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**
+ The paper is well organized and easy to follow.
+ It is interesting to discuss the pretrained model on noisy large-scale datasets regardless of issues in motivations/techniques/results (see details in Weaknesses and Feedback).

**Weaknesses and Feedback**
1. Motivation and concepts of co-training can be elaborated to improve clarity.

    a. Please clarify what the "complementary nature" of three losses (or training strategies) are, and how they can lead to a co-training strategy in order to tackle Internet data.
    
    b. Please tell the differences between the referred "co-training" in this paper vs conventional co-training in machine learning.  The later is a semi-supervised learning technique that requires two views of the data.  Co-training in this paper is closer to a joint learning of three losses.  Please clarify their differences to avoid tentative abuse of terms.

2. Method requires better rationale for the design choice.

    a. Sec 3.1-3.3: The relationship between the three losses and their effects on noisy Internet data is unclear.  These sections (3.1-3.3) reiterate existing arts, and can use more rationale for the design choice to avoid trivial combination (eg, how the three losses complement each other by nature as the authors claimed).

    b. The authors claim that the three losses ($L_{cont}$, $L_{corr}$, $L_{pred}$) are complementary based on the observation that adding $L_{corr}$ and/or $L_{pred}$ to $L_{cont}$ will improve the performance (Sec 3.4).  However, adding all three losses could slightly regress the performance (from 11.6->11.5).  Please add analysis and provide justifications of which cases these losses complement each other.

    c. Similar to 2.a, the intended "co-training" is closer to loss re-weighting through hyper-parameters, which are empirically set to (1, 1, 200).  This can be an abused term from the conventional co-training and requires justification of design choice (eg, how many degrees of the losses magnitudes are away from each other).

    d. The assumptions of the proposed CALI-NCE require more discussion.  While contrastive loss may suffer from false positives/negatives, it is unclear how adding cross entropy (joint training) could alleviate the issue.  Please enrich the explanation and clarify why adding cross entropy helps pull two videos together.

    e. The statement that "... does not add on dot product and provides model flexibility for training" needs elaboration.  While the correspondence removes the dot product, it is unclear if removing dot products improves model efficiency and/or effectiveness.  Please add rationale / analysis to better support this claim. 

    f. Considering "correspondence can be considered as a weak label", please explain why the outputs of correspondence modeling are more accurate supervision signals.

    g. It is unclear how $\hat{c_{ii}}$ is obtained (eg, from the previous epoch of training?).  Please clarify.

3. Experiments

    a. Please clarify if “ours” in Tables 2-7 represents "L_pred+L_CaliNCE" or "L_cont+L_corr+L_pred".  In addition, metrics R@ are interchangeably used with  accuracy throughout the paper.  Please check if the use of accuracy in GDT (Patrick et.al., 2020a) equals to R@, and be consistent when referring them.

    b. The baseline CLIP is missing in SoTA comparisons (eg, Tables 2-4).  It seems that the proposed method underperforms the baseline CLIP.  Eg, the proposed method obtains 34.4/64.2, which is worse than 46.1/73.0 [r1,r2] by CLIP (only with contrastive loss) pre-trained on YFCC100M (an image-caption dataset, also crawled from web).  This is a bit surprising given that CLIP is only trained with contrastive loss (vs 3 losses proposed by authors) and only images (vs videos used in this work).

[r1] Multimodal Open-Vocabulary Video Classification via Pre-Trained Vision and Language Models, Arxiv, 2022.\
[r2] https://github.com/openai/CLIP
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Overall the paper is well organized and easy to read.  However, the current manuscript would need to improve motivation (complementary nature / co-training), rationale for novelty (design choice), and comparisons / analysis against the baseline methods.  From current descriptions, the readers should be able to reproduce this work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper addresses the problem of video-language representation learning. Existing approaches typically employed one of the following approaches: 1) correspondence modeling, where the model was trained using a video-text match/no-match classification task, 2) contrastive learning, where model was trained by contrasting positive and negative video-text pairs, and 3) predictive coding, where model was trained by minimizing text and video embedding L2 distance. The authors proposed an approach that combined these three objectives by using correspondence loss to weight the contrastive NCE loss. They demonstrated its performance on three main tasks, namely text-video retrieval, action recognition, video-to-video retrieval, and showed improvement over the selected baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
[Strength] The authors conducted solid experiments to show the interaction between threes approaches mentioned above, which explained clearly the motivation for their combined loss. 
[Strength] The authors reported numbers across various standard benchmarks such as MSR-VTT, HDMB, UCF, and MSVD and provided insightful observations on the results.
[Weakness] The main issue with this paper is comparison to lower baselines. For example, on HMDB, recognition performance of this work is 49% while in [1] is 60.8% (ViT-B/16). Or on MSR VTT, zero-shot retrieval, this work is 13.1% (Table 2) vs. [2], which also pretrained on Webvid-2M, is >23% (Table 4).

[1] Multimodal Open-Vocabulary Video Classification via Pre-Trained Vision and Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.07646v1 
[2] Frozen in Time: A Joint Video and Image Encoder for End-to-End Retrieval. ICCV2021. https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.00650v2
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper was written with clarity and it is easy to follow. 
This work should be easy to reproduce since  implementation details were provided.   
The novelty is limited since only main idea is using the video-text correspondence score to re-weight the NCE loss.
content.summary_of_the_review: While I like the clear presentation and the provided insights of this paper, my main concern, as mentioned in the weaknesses above, is that its performance is too far below the current state of the art. Until this work can close the big gaps, at least, for certain benchmark, it is hard for me to justify an acceptance.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper aims to tackle the false positive and false negatives issue for improving the performance of video representation learning. To this end, the authors propose first estimating the confidence of video-text pairs by using the probability output by the visual-textual matching modules. After that, the estimated confidences are used to penalize the false positives in the contrastive learning paradigm. To verify the effectiveness of the proposed method, multiple downstream tasks are performed including text-to-video retrieval, video action recognition, and video retrieval.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The studied problem is interesting and valuable. Actually, false positive and false negative issues are practical in video representation learning.
2. Revisiting the cross-modal representation learning paradigm might bring some insights to the community. 

Weaknesses:
1. My major concern is the novelty of this paper. This paper takes a lot of space in Method to explain three popular kinds of video representation learning paradigms and proposes the so-called co-training manner that simply combines two paradigms together. Actually, the so-called co-training manner is widely-used in the multi-modal pertaining community where the contrastive loss and ITM loss are usually used together to boost performance. Therefore, the reviewer cannot regard the so-called co-training manner as one contribution of this paper. More importantly, although the studied false positive and false negative issues are interesting and practical for video representation learning, the proposed method and actual effect lack novelty and guarantee. First, this paper tries to tackle the false positive issue by penalizing the unconfident positive pairs. Such a reweighting strategy on contrastive loss is not new and has been used in other cross-modal learning methods such as [1]. Second, the authors claim that both the false positive and false negative issues are solved using the predicted correspondence confidence in Fig. 3. However, the reviewer cannot understand why the false negative issue can also be tackled by using the estimated confidences
[1] Robust Audio-Visual Instance Discrimination, CVPR 2021
2. The other concern is the effectiveness of the proposed method. As shown in Table 2-5, the compared baselines are all before 2021. The recently proposed video representation learning methods should be included to further show the effectiveness. Second, as shown in Table 7, the proposed method owns limited robustness improvement compared to the baseline even in the hand-crafted high noise scenario (50%). The reviewer doubts the robustness and necessity of the proposed method which penalizes the noisy pair by using the predicted correspondence confidences
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Quality: The paper is likely to have a modest impact on the video representation learning community. 
Clarity: The paper is well organized but the presentation has minor details that could be improved.
Originality: The main ideas of the paper are not novel or have limited novelty. Please see the weaknesses.
content.summary_of_the_review: Although the studied problem is practical for the video representation learning community, it is no new and has been studied during past years. Besides, the proposed method has limited novelty.

content.title: Cali-NCE: Boosting Cross-modal Video Representation Learning with Calibrated Alignment
content.abstract: With the large-scale video-text datasets being collected, learning general visual-textual representation has gained increasing attention. While recent methods are designed with the assumption that the alt-text description naturally conveys the meaning and context of the video in semantics (i.e. well aligned with each other), it is unlikely to be satisfied for the Internet data, which potentially harms the quality of the learned visual-textual representation. To address this challenge,  we first revisit three mainstream approaches: correspondence modeling, contrastive learning and predictive coding, demonstrating that a simple co-training strategy with these methods leads to a clear improvement in performance. To further explore the complementary nature of different training strategies, we propose a simple yet effective joint training framework that factorizes the total objective into conditional ones, termed as Cali-NCE. Specifically, the correspondence between video and text descriptions is firstly estimated with a correspondence score, which is later used to calibrate the sample weightings during contrastive training. Through extensive experiments, we show that the proposed approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple downstream tasks: text-to-video retrieval, video action recognition, and video retrieval. Code and models will be made publicly available.
